evals.prompt: I run DevRel at Loomcast, a webhook delivery platform. We published a post called "How we cut webhook retry storms by 90%" - 2,100 words, sections are Background, Why retries storm, Our old queue, What we tried first, The token bucket fix, Benchmarks, Conclusion. I want to turn it into a polished animated explainer, about 3 minutes, live on our site by the 24th because that's when the new retry API goes GA. It's me and one other person, neither of us can make diagrams or motion graphics, and we have no video editor. What's the script?
evals.expected_output: A shape decision that deletes the constraint-ruled-out shapes out loud, ranks the survivors, re-ranks against the hard GA date, transposes the post into claims rather than section headings, and returns a beat sheet built on the surviving shape.
expectations: States the promise as a single sentence naming one specific viewer and the one specific thing the video shows working.
Deletes the concept explainer from the shape menu because nobody can produce diagrams, rather than ranking it low or last.
Names which shapes were deleted out loud instead of silently omitting them.
States the shape ranking and the final pick explicitly rather than presenting a single shape as the only option.
Ranks shapes by production effort and value returned per unit of that effort, not by their runtime bands.
Treats the GA date on the 24th as a constraint that promotes the changelog/release clip and the error/fix shape.
Treats the GA date as a reason to delete the deep dive outright rather than to shorten it.
Lists what the post proves as claims and discards the post's section headings as the video's structure.
Drops or compresses the Background and "What we tried first" sections instead of giving each one a beat.
Puts the measured 90% figure on screen twice - once as the problem, once as the proof - rather than only mentioning it in narration.
Invents no figure, customer, persona or call to action that the request did not supply.
Returns a beat table whose columns include visual, on-screen action, narration, starting state, estimated seconds, and a core-or-cuttable marking.
Treats "polished" as an unusable adjective, converting it into a concrete decision (a runtime, a viewer, an on-screen artefact) or asking for one, rather than designing to it.

evals.prompt: Here's the first 90 seconds of our screencast for Parsel, our CSV parsing library. 0:00-0:07 animated logo with music. 0:07-0:20 "Hey everyone, welcome back to the Parsel channel, hope you're having a great week." 0:20-0:35 "Today we're looking at streaming parsers, which are a really important topic." 0:35-1:20 npm install, creating the project folder, opening the editor, pasting the config. At 1:20 the first parse actually runs. Analytics say 38% of people are still there at 30 seconds and the curve is flat after that. What do I do with the intro?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the payoff sits outside the measured intro window, plus a rewritten opening beat that does all four opening jobs inside 30 seconds and relocates the setup.
expectations: Identifies that the entire payoff sits outside the first 30 seconds of the video.
Names the 30-second mark as the boundary the video platform's own retention report measures the intro against, not as a stylistic preference.
Moves the working result into the first beat so a parse is already running on screen.
Requires the opening to name the problem in the viewer's own words.
Requires the opening to show the result actually running rather than promising it.
Requires the opening to state the prerequisites so the wrong viewer leaves early instead of dropping minutes in.
Requires the opening to state the runtime.
Caps ceremony - logo, music, greeting - at roughly five seconds.
Presents the roughly-five-second ceremony figure as a measured perception threshold rather than a hard cutoff.
Moves the npm install and project setup after the payoff or into a companion repository.
Invents no retention benchmark and promises no specific percentage the reshoot will reach.
Delivers the new opening as actual spoken narration lines paired with what is on screen, not as a list of advice.

evals.prompt: Writing a 4-minute walkthrough of our new query builder at Fernwood Data. Just give me the narration, I'll wing the screen stuff while I record - I've done this a dozen times. The flow is: show the old way with raw SQL strings, show the builder syntax, run it against the sample database, show the generated SQL, then show the type errors it catches.
evals.expected_output: A full beat sheet rather than a narration-only script, with per-beat starting states that stand alone, per-beat duration estimates including dead time, core/cuttable markings, a cut plan and task-shaped chapter titles.
expectations: Delivers a beat table rather than a narration-only script, despite the request for narration only.
Gives every beat a visual and an on-screen action kept in columns separate from the narration.
Gives every beat a starting state precise enough to re-shoot that beat alone.
Ensures no beat's starting state depends on a previous beat's live output.
Gives every beat an estimated duration.
Marks every beat core or cuttable.
Sizes each beat to roughly one thought and about twenty seconds of narration.
Splits any beat that could not be recorded in a single pass into two beats.
Produces a cut plan naming which beats go first if the runtime overruns.
States that cutting every cuttable beat still delivers the promise.
Explains that the cut decision belongs in the script before recording rather than at edit time.
Gives each segment a chapter title phrased as a task or outcome rather than "Part 1" or "Step 2".
Includes per-beat dead time such as query runs and page loads in the estimates instead of counting narration alone.

evals.prompt: My script for the Halyard CLI tutorial has 1,640 words of narration across 19 beats. Target runtime is 9 minutes. Assume the standard 150 words per minute for a tech video and tell me whether I'm over. Also, should I just talk faster to squeeze under? I've read that faster is better for retention.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to compute runtime from an assumed rate, an instruction to measure the recorder's own rate and add per-beat dead time, a rejection of speaking faster as a lever, and segmentation advice for a 9-minute target.
expectations: Refuses to compute the runtime from a table value or an assumed words-per-minute figure.
Instructs the user to measure the recorder's own speaking rate, for example by timing a read of a fixed passage.
States that estimated dead time must be added per beat on top of the narration time.
Names concrete dead-time sources such as builds, installs, page loads and deliberate pauses.
Declines to endorse speaking faster as a retention lever.
Explains that the published speaking-rate-to-engagement correlation is a surface proxy for enthusiasm rather than a lever to pull.
Advises bringing energy instead of forcing speed.
States that cuts happen before recording, never in the edit.
Declines to return a single confident runtime number, saying the measured rate and per-beat dead-time estimates are required first.
Recommends splitting a 9-minute target into chaptered segments of roughly six minutes or less, citing the published median-engagement evidence rather than an invented benchmark.

evals.prompt: Here's the narration for our webhook signing screencast at Tidewater. Legal says it has to be accessible, so I've budgeted to record a separate audio description track after the edit is locked. The lines are: "Okay so as you can see here we've got the handler." / "Now I'll just change this to that." / "Click here, and then over here." / "And there we go, it works now." / "This function does a bunch of stuff under the hood." Is the narration ready to record?
evals.expected_output: Every line rejected as deictic and rewritten to name the identifier, value, destination or observable result, plus integrated description replacing the planned separate track, an audio-only pass, and caption correction against the narration column.
expectations: Rejects all five quoted lines as deictic narration that carries no information without the picture.
Rewrites each quoted line into a version naming the identifier, value, screen or result out loud.
Replaces "click here, and then over here" with named UI destinations rather than screen positions.
Replaces "it works now" with the observable evidence - a status code, an output line, a test result - instead of the conclusion.
States that the visual information belongs inside the main narration rather than in a separate description track.
Identifies a separate audio-description track as the retrofit for material that already exists, not the approach for a video still being scripted.
Notes that doing this at script time is far cheaper than bolting a description onto a finished recording.
Prescribes an audio-only pass: reading the narration column with the screen off and rewriting every sentence that stops meaning something.
Notes that captions are required for prerecorded synchronized media at WCAG Level A.
Instructs auto-generating the captions and correcting them against the narration column rather than re-transcribing the video.
Notes that deictic lines also make an auto-generated caption track unusable.

evals.prompt: Our "Deploy your first service on Tessellate" video is 11 minutes. Structure: 0:00 intro, 0:20 I read out the agenda, 0:35 to 2:10 how our scheduler and control plane work, then eight deploy steps that each start with "so now that we've done that", then a recap at the end. No chapters. Average view duration is 2 minutes 40. My plan is to cut it to 7 minutes by trimming the architecture part and speeding up the delivery. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of runtime as the fix, identifying addressability as the real defect, backed by the procedural-video evidence, with titled segments, per-segment starting states, state sentences replacing back-references and a valid chapter list.
expectations: Identifies the problem as addressability rather than runtime.
Cites that tutorials are watched roughly two to three minutes on average regardless of their total length.
Treats the 2:40 average view duration as consistent with normal procedural-video use rather than as proof of a pacing failure.
Notes that procedural video is re-watched and paused selectively at step boundaries rather than watched once end to end.
Cuts the video into titled segments, roughly one per deploy step.
Titles segments in the viewer's search vocabulary as tasks or outcomes, never "Step 4" or "Part 2".
Gives each segment a starting state so a returning viewer can enter in the middle.
Replaces every "so now that we've done that" transition with a sentence stating the current state.
Moves the architecture background to a linked written page, keeping only the sentence the deploy itself needs.
Notes that the runtime barely needs to move for the fix to work.
Adds a chapter list whose first timestamp is 00:00, with at least three entries, each at least ten seconds long, in ascending order.
Declines speeding up the delivery as a remedy.

evals.prompt: Kestrel Analytics ships v4.2 on the 3rd. The changelog entry reads: "Saved views can now be shared with a read-only link that expires." I want a 75-second clip for the release post and the product feed. Give me the script with the chapter markers and timestamps.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to produce a chapter list for a clip under the platform's three-timestamp minimum, the platform's chapter rules stated, description and clip metadata delivered instead, and a single-change beat sheet opening on the change working in the product.
expectations: Declines to produce a chapter list for a 75-second clip.
Explains that the clip falls under the platform's minimum of three chapter timestamps.
States the platform's chapter requirements: first timestamp 00:00, at least three timestamps, each chapter ten seconds or longer, listed in ascending order.
Notes the platform revises these rules and that they should be re-checked before publishing, or says plainly that they were not re-verified.
Delivers the description and clip metadata in place of the chapter list.
Keeps the clip to the single change, covering no second feature.
Opens on the change working inside the product rather than on a title card, a logo or a feature list.
Sizes the production effort as roughly an hour over a changelog entry someone already wrote.
Notes the clip is embargoed until the release actually ships on the 3rd.
Marks each beat core or cuttable and names a starting state for each.

evals.prompt: For our Rowan SDK launch video we hired a videographer with a 4K cinema rig and studio lighting, two days of shooting booked. My plan is to type the whole integration file live on camera starting from the imports, about 60 lines, talking continuously so there's never any dead air, then run it at the end. Anything I'm missing?
evals.expected_output: A correction that studio production values buy nothing, that code screencasts are the weaker format and need compensating signaling, plus specific pacing rules: no boilerplate typed, narrate before the reveal, a scripted silent hold after results, diffs over whole files, and stated legibility floors.
expectations: States that studio production values showed no measured engagement benefit.
Notes that code screencasts sat in the weaker bucket of the published instructional-format comparison.
Cites that continuous tablet-drawing style tutorials held roughly 1.5 to 2 times the normalized engagement of code screencasts.
Recommends annotating or drawing on top of the code rather than leaving the frame bare.
Names the compensating levers as motion, annotation, zoom and a face cut in at deliberate moments.
Notes that interspersing the presenter's face with the other visuals is a measured improvement over slides alone.
Rejects typing the imports and boilerplate live, prescribing pre-supplied, pasted or snippet-expanded code instead.
Limits live typing to the lines the video is actually about.
Instructs narrating before the reveal rather than talking over the viewer's reading.
Prescribes a scripted silent hold after a result appears so the viewer can read the output.
Identifies filling that pause with commentary as exactly the defect the "never any dead air" plan creates.
Recommends showing the diff or the smallest fragment that carries the point rather than the whole 60-line file.
Gives legibility floors of at least 24pt terminal text and at least 20pt editor text while labelling them as this skill's own baseline rather than a published standard.

evals.prompt: A contractor wrote this script for our "Migrate from v2 to v3" video and I don't love it. Can you rewrite it so it's punchier? Beats: 1) the v2 config file on screen. 2) "The v2 loader resolved paths relative to the working directory, which broke in monorepos." 3) three sentences re-describing the config file we just looked at. 4) "So here's the new resolver" then straight into "and that's why builds are deterministic now". 5) a 60-word sentence with three subordinate clauses about the cache. 6) a side note about a Windows path bug we hit. 7) the call to action. He also claims monorepo builds got 4x faster.
evals.expected_output: A graded diagnosis rather than a rewrite: a beat table, findings mapped to logic break, density drop and unspeakable line, risk levels, original lines shown beside proposed replacements, and the author's 4x claim left untouched.
expectations: Diagnoses the script beat by beat instead of returning a rewritten script.
Asks what the format is - talking head, screencast, silent captioned clip - before judging the beats.
Tables the beats with a number, topic, function and status per row.
Grades each finding as high, medium or low risk rather than listing findings flat.
Flags beat 4 as a logic break with a missing bridging sentence between the new resolver and deterministic builds.
Flags beat 3 as a density drop that repeats what the screen already showed.
Flags beat 5 as an unspeakable line, too long or tangled to read aloud in one breath.
Shows the original line beside the proposed replacement rather than overwriting the contractor's text.
Checks whether the Windows path aside in beat 6 is load-bearing argument before recommending a cut.
Leaves the 4x claim alone as the author's own, judging how it is said rather than whether it is true.
Manufactures no findings against beats that are fine.
Offers the marked-up script as an optional next step instead of delivering a rewrite unasked.

evals.prompt: I'm putting a slide in front of our VP to get budget for a video program. I need hard numbers with sources: how long videos should be, what font size to use for code on screen, how many seconds the intro gets, and any industry standards on engagement. Give me something I can cite in the deck.
evals.expected_output: A citation list that separates externally published findings from this skill's own self-set baselines, states each source's limitations, and warns against presenting a self-set number as an industry standard.
expectations: Separates externally published findings from this skill's own self-set baselines rather than presenting one undifferentiated list.
Labels the 24pt terminal and 20pt editor figures as self-set baselines, not an industry standard.
Attributes the median-engagement and length findings to the large MOOC instructional-video study, including its session count.
States the finding that median engagement time is at most about six minutes regardless of total video length.
States that viewers typically get less than halfway through videos longer than nine minutes.
States the study's own limitations: a retrospective log study rather than an experiment, on a MOOC corpus.
States that watch time is a proxy for engagement and that engagement is not learning.
Declines to cite the widely circulated 100%/50%/20% engagement table as a finding, or flags it as a secondary rendering of a normalized plot.
Attributes the 52% engagement rate for under-one-minute videos to the hosted-video industry report and flags it as a business-video corpus rather than a teaching one.
Identifies the 30-second intro window as a measurement boundary defined by the video platform's retention report.
Attributes the roughly five-second ceremony threshold to a usability finding about perceived intro length rather than to a style rule.
Labels the roughly six-minute segment ceiling as this skill's own baseline, applied at the segment level rather than the video level.
Warns that presenting a self-set number as an industry standard will fail in a review once someone checks it.

evals.prompt: We need a video for the Cardinal 2.0 launch on the 19th. Make it great - something really engaging and technical that shows off the whole platform. Can you write it?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to draft anything before the promise, viewer and source are established, delivered as a one-question-at-a-time interview with multiple-choice options and the request's adjectives rejected.
expectations: Refuses to write the script before the promise, the viewer and the source material are established.
Asks questions one at a time rather than sending a block of questions at once.
Offers multiple-choice options on the questions where options exist.
Refuses "great", "engaging" and "technical" as answers and converts each into a concrete decision.
Asks what the source material is - a published post or docs page, a changelog or pull request, a working demo, a recorded talk, or nothing written yet.
Asks what the viewer should be able to do or decide when the video ends.
Asks who is watching, offering named audience options such as evaluator, user hitting an error, existing user or buyer-adjacent viewer.
Asks about the effort ceiling and whether the video is a one-off launch win or a compounding asset.
Produces no draft script, opening beat or finished shape recommendation in this turn.
Invents no pain statement, metric, persona or call to action.
States that anything inferred rather than stated by the user will be marked unconfirmed in the draft.

evals.prompt: Northgate Ledger is enterprise reconciliation software - every deal goes through procurement and a security review. A solutions engineer is recording a 5-minute walkthrough on her work laptop against our staging tenant, which has three real pilot customers' data loaded in it. We ship v7.3 next month but the demo box already runs v7.4-rc. What do I need to hand her before she records, and how will I know afterwards whether it worked?
evals.expected_output: A recording brief with seeded data replacing customer records, an off-limits list, one-command starting states rehearsed cold, credential and hygiene rules, the version mismatch stated aloud, and KPIs compared against the company's own prior videos of the same shape.
expectations: Requires the three pilot customers' data to be replaced with seeded data before recording rather than edited out afterwards.
Lists customer names, tenant IDs, internal hostnames and pricing as off-limits on screen.
Flags the v7.4-rc versus v7.3 mismatch and requires the version to be stated aloud in the narration.
Requires limitations to be stated aloud, because an over-claim in a video outlives the release it described.
Notes the recording will be replayed in a procurement or security review where verbal hedging is not visible.
Delivers a recording brief with one starting-state command per beat.
Requires each starting state to be rehearsed from a machine that has not already run the demo.
Requires throwaway credentials that get rotated after the recording.
Requires notifications, badges and personal browser-profile artefacts to be off at the OS level rather than minimized.
Requires every slow operation - installs, builds, image pulls - to happen before recording starts.
Compares the resulting metrics against the company's own previous videos of the same shape rather than an external or invented benchmark.
Names takes-per-beat during recording as a script defect signal, usually an unrealistic starting state, rather than a presenter performance problem.
